A vast, ring-shaped region of space containing countless irregularly shaped bodies of rock and metal, often the primordial remnants of a planetary system that failed to form a planet.
A celestial body orbiting a star that is massive enough to be rounded by its own gravity, but has not cleared its neighboring region of other objects. Pluto is a famous example.
A terrestrial planet composed primarily of silicate rocks or metals. They have a solid surface, making them potential candidates for complex geology and, under the right conditions, life.
A cosmic "snowball" of frozen gases, rock, and dust. As it nears a star, it heats up and begins to outgas, displaying a visible atmosphere (coma) and sometimes a tail of gas and dust.

A massive planet composed mainly of hydrogen, helium, and other gases, lacking a well-defined solid surface. They possess immense gravitational fields and often host extensive systems of rings and moons.

A "failed star" with insufficient mass to sustain hydrogen fusion. It occupies the boundary between a gas giant and a true star, glowing dimly from the heat of its formation and limited deuterium fusion.

A small, cool, and incredibly long-lived star. Its slow rate of fusion allows it to burn for trillions of years, far longer than the current age of the universe, making them the most common type of star.
The dense, compact remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel. Composed mostly of electron-degenerate matter, it shines with leftover thermal energy, slowly fading over billions of years.
A stable, main-sequence star, like our own Sun. It fuses hydrogen into helium for billions of years, creating a wide habitable zone suitable for a diverse system.
The late-stage evolution of a sun-like star. Having exhausted the hydrogen in its core, it begins fusing hydrogen in a surrounding shell, causing it to expand dramatically and cool its surface.
An evolved, massive star in its final stages. It has swelled to an immense size, with a cool surface temperature and powerful stellar winds that shed its outer layers into space.
